entry: U.S. federal law prohibiting [[Discrimination|discrimination]] based on race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. It also barred unequal application of voter registration requirements, racial segregation in schools and public accommodations, and employment discrimination. Proposed by [[John F. Kennedy|President John F. Kennedy]] in June 1963, the bill faced a 72-day Senate filibuster before the Senate passed it on June 19, 1964. After Kennedy's assassination on November 22, 1963, President [[Lyndon B. Johnson]] pushed the bill forward and signed it on July 2, 1964.

Class of rights that protect individuals from infringement by governments, social organizations, and private individuals. Civil rights include physical and mental integrity, life, and safety, along with [[Discrimination|protection from discrimination]], [[Privacy|privacy]], and freedom of thought, speech, religion, press, assembly, and movement. Political rights include procedural fairness, such as a fair trial and due process, and participation in [[Civil society|civil society]] and [[Politics|politics]] through association, assembly, petition, and voting. These rights form the original core of [[Human rights|international human rights]] and the first portion of the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]] (1948). Under the theory of negative and positive rights, they are generally considered negative rights.

Legal system rooted in the [[Roman Empire]]. Today it is the world's most common legal system, practiced in about 150 countries. It was comprehensively codified starting in the 19th century, most notably in France's [[Napoleonic Code]] (1804) and Germany's *Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch* (1900). Unlike [[Common law|common law]] systems, which rely on [[Precedent|judicial precedent]], civil law treats legal codes as the primary source of law and gives case law a secondary role. Its codes set out general principles in concise, broadly applicable articles rather than fact-specific rules. Civil law is often paired with the inquisitorial system, though the terms are not synonymous. Its historical roots include the [[Corpus Juris Civilis]], compiled under Justinian I between 529 and 534, along with Napoleonic, Germanic, canonical, and feudal influences.

Fundamental individual rights and freedoms that governments pledge not to restrict without due process of law. They often include freedom of conscience, press, [[Freedom of religion|religion]], expression, and assembly, as well as personal security, [[Privacy|privacy]], equality before the law, a fair trial, and life. Scope differs by country, and property rights, reproductive rights, and civil marriage are disputed as civil liberties. Libertarians emphasize minimal government intervention in personal and economic affairs. [[John Stuart Mill]] argued in *On Liberty* for protecting individuals from government encroachment, and [[Friedrich Hayek]] warned in *The Road to Serfdom* against expanding state power. China's constitution guarantees civil liberties, but critics say subversion and state-secrets clauses are used to imprison critics of the [[Chinese Communist Party]].

Social movement in the United States, 1954–1968, against legal racial segregation, discrimination, and disenfranchisement. Its roots lay in the [[Reconstruction era]], in the 1940s, and in Mahatma Gandhi's nonviolent movement in India. Using boycotts, sit-ins, marches, and civil disobedience, the movement was led by figures including [[Martin Luther King Jr.|Martin Luther King Jr.]] and won federal laws including the [[Civil Rights Act of 1964|Civil Rights Act of 1964]], the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and the Fair Housing Act of 1968. From the mid-1960s, the Black power movement, shaped by [[Malcolm X]] and the [[Black Panther Party]], criticized the movement's moderate, incremental tendencies. Civil unrest in Black communities between 1964 and 1969, peaking in 1967 and after King's assassination in 1968, weakened support from White moderates. Racial gaps in income, housing, education, and criminal justice persisted into the early 21st century.

Worldwide series of political movements for equality before the law, peaking in the 1960s. Many used nonviolent protest and civil resistance, though some were accompanied by civil unrest or armed rebellion. Many have not fully achieved their goals, but have improved the legal rights of some previously oppressed groups in some places. The [[Civil rights movement|American civil rights movement]] (1954–1968) and similar movements sought equal legal protection for all, including minorities, [[Women's rights|women]], people with disabilities, and LGBT people. In [[Northern Ireland]], a civil rights campaign in the late 1960s and early 1970s modeled itself on the American movement and demanded an end to discrimination in housing and local government, and an end to [[Gerrymandering|gerrymandering]] that limited Catholic voting. Violence escalated during the [[The Troubles|Troubles]], and the Provisional Irish Republican Army rose from the Catholic community.

Career government personnel, hired rather than elected, whose tenure usually survives changes of political leadership. Civil servants work at any level of government and, in a healthy system, answer to the government rather than to a [[Political party|political party]]. The term varies by country. In the United Kingdom, only national government employees are called civil servants, while local government staff are called local government officers. The concept arose in China, and the modern civil service developed in Britain in the 18th century. International civil servants, employed by intergovernmental bodies such as the [[United Nations]], are governed by internal staff regulations rather than national law.

Third sector of society, distinct from [[Government|government]] and business and including the family and the private sphere. Some definitions describe it as the aggregate of [[Non-governmental organization|nongovernmental organizations]] and institutions that advance citizens' interests, or as individuals and organizations independent of government. Others use the term for elements of a [[Democracy|democratic]] society, such as free speech and an independent judiciary. Scholars do not agree on a single understanding. The concept's literature has origins in Scottish Enlightenment philosophy and in the work of Hegel, [[Alexis de Tocqueville|Tocqueville]], and [[Karl Marx|Marx]]. In the late 20th century, [[Václav Havel|Václav Havel]] and other Eastern European dissidents used the term for civic associations threatened by communist states. Researchers Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba argued that civil society helps citizens become better informed, make better voting choices, and hold government accountable.

War between organized groups within the same state or country. Its aim may be to take control of the country or a region, achieve independence for a region, or change government policies. Most modern civil wars involve intervention by outside powers. According to Patrick M. Regan, about two thirds of the 138 intrastate conflicts between the end of [[World War II]] and 2000 involved international intervention. Civil wars often involve regular armed forces and large numbers of casualties. Since 1945 they have caused over 25 million deaths and forced the displacement of millions more. Civil wars averaged just over four years after World War II, compared with one-and-a-half years in 1900–1944. Nations including [[Somalia]], Burma (Myanmar), [[Uganda]], and [[Angola]] were considered to have promising futures before civil wars engulfed them.

Group of organisms comprising a common ancestor and all of its descendants. Also called a monophyletic group, a clade is the fundamental unit of cladistics, a modern approach to [[Taxonomy|taxonomy]] adopted by most biological fields. The ancestor may be an individual, a population, or an extinct or living [[Species|species]]. Clades nest within one another as branches split. The term was coined in 1957 by Julian Huxley for the result of cladogenesis, the evolutionary splitting of a parent species into two.

Group of people united by actual or perceived [[Kinship|kinship]] and descent. Members may claim descent from a founding or apical ancestor who symbolizes the group's unity. Traditional anthropology classified such ancestors, frequently animals, as [[Totem|totems]]. In many societies, exogamy rules apply by clan, so members are excluded from marriage with their own clan, or with the clans of their parents or grandparents, as [[Incest|incest]]. Often a clan is a smaller, integral part of a larger society such as a [[Tribe|tribe]], chiefdom, or state. The word derives from the Gaelic *clann*, meaning children or descendants, and entered English around 1406 as a label for society in the Scottish Highlands. Clans also exist in Irish, Chinese, Korean, and Japanese society, and in post-Soviet countries the term describes informal networks.

German virtuoso pianist, composer, and piano teacher of the Romantic era. Born in [[Leipzig]] to a musical family, she was trained as a child prodigy by her father, Friedrich Wieck, and began touring at age eleven. Her concert career spanned 61 years and helped change the piano recital by lessening the importance of purely virtuosic works. She married composer [[Robert Schumann]] in 1840; the couple had eight children and encouraged [[Johannes Brahms]]. After her husband's death, she continued touring for decades, and from 1878 she taught at Dr. Hoch's Konservatorium in [[Frankfurt]], attracting international students. She also edited her husband's published works. Her compositions include solo piano pieces, a piano concerto, chamber music, choral pieces, and songs.

Single-reed [[Woodwind instrument|woodwind]] instrument with a nearly cylindrical bore and a flared bell. The clarinet family is the largest woodwind family, ranging from contrabass to piccolo sizes, and the B♭ soprano clarinet is the most common type. German instrument maker Johann Christoph Denner is generally credited with inventing the clarinet around 1700 by adding a register key to the chalumeau, an earlier single-reed instrument. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed his Concerto for Clarinet and Orchestra in A major in 1791 for the basset clarinet, an extended instrument. In 1812 Iwan Müller presented a clarinet with seven finger holes and 13 keys. Today the clarinet is a standard fixture of the [[Orchestra|orchestra]] and concert band, used in [[Classical music|classical music]], military bands, [[Jazz|jazz]], klezmer, and other styles.

American film actor often referred to as the "King of Hollywood." He appeared in more than 60 motion pictures over a 37-year career, three decades of which he spent as a leading man. Gable won the Academy Award for Best Actor for [[Frank Capra|Frank Capra's]] *It Happened One Night* (1934) and earned further Best Actor nominations for *Mutiny on the Bounty* (1935) and *Gone with the Wind* (1939). His other notable films include *Call of the Wild* (1935) and *Mogambo* (1953). His final onscreen role was in [[John Huston|John Huston's]] *The Misfits* (1961). He appeared 16 times on Quigley Publishing's annual Top Ten Money Making Stars poll. In 1999 the American Film Institute ranked him seventh-greatest male screen legend of classical Hollywood cinema.

[[Prejudice|Prejudice]] or discrimination on the basis of social class, also called classism. It includes individual attitudes and behaviors, and systems of policies and practices that benefit the upper class at the expense of the lower class. [[Social class|Social class]] is a hierarchy based on wealth, income, education, occupation, and social network. In India, Singapore, Bangladesh, and Pakistan, classism intersects with [[Caste|caste]] and persists within diasporic communities despite being illegal in host countries. Class discrimination also intersects with [[Racism|racism]] and [[Sexism|sexism]]. Women make up nearly two-thirds of workers in the 20 occupations with the lowest median wages for full-time, year-round employees. Modern classism is harder to identify because class structures are less rigid, and experiences of discrimination are often subtle.

Branch of [[Algebraic number theory|algebraic number theory]] concerned with abelian extensions. It describes all abelian Galois extensions of local and global fields using objects associated with the ground field. A key result is Artin reciprocity, which gives a canonical isomorphism between the Galois group of a finite abelian extension and a quotient of the idele class group. The theory takes its name from class fields, the abelian extensions that correspond to open subgroups of finite index. [[David Hilbert|David Hilbert]] conjectured results that Takagi and Artin later proved, with the help of Chebotarev's theorem. Explicit class field theory includes the Kronecker–Weber theorem, which describes the abelian extensions of ℚ. The theory has three main generalizations: higher class field theory, the Langlands program, and anabelian geometry.

Standardized literary form of Arabic, also called Quranic Arabic, used from the 7th century throughout the [[Middle Ages]]. It was used in Umayyad and Abbasid poetry, elevated prose, and oratory, and it is the liturgical language of [[Islam|Islam]]. Modern Standard Arabic is its direct descendant, used in writing and formal speech across the Arab world. Modern Standard Arabic uses a subset of the syntactic structures of Classical Arabic, but their morphology and syntax remain basically unchanged. Both are normally called *al-fuṣḥā*, meaning the most eloquent. Classical Arabic is considered a conservative [[Semitic languages|Semitic]] language; it preserved the three Proto-Semitic grammatical cases and their declension. The [[Arabic script|Arabic script]] is generally believed to have evolved from local cursive varieties of the [[Aramaic]] script.

City-state of ancient Greece in the peninsula of Attica. Athenian democracy was established in 508 BC and lasted almost two centuries, with a few brief interruptions. Cleisthenes's reforms replaced four traditional tribes with ten new ones, and the Assembly was open to all full citizens. Athens led the [[Delian League|Delian League]], which reached its peak in the 450s and 440s BC during the age of [[Pericles|Pericles]]. In the [[Peloponnesian War|Peloponnesian War]] (431–404 BC), Athens fought [[Sparta|Sparta]]-led forces and suffered a decisive defeat in 404 BC. After the battle of Chaeronea, [[Philip II of Macedon|Philip II of Macedon]] forced Athens into the League of Corinth. Athens was a center of the arts, learning, and philosophy, and is widely referred to as a cradle of Western civilization.

Style of written Chinese in which the classics of Chinese literature were composed, from about the 5th century BC. For millennia afterward, scholars imitated its [[Syntax|syntax]] in a form called Literary Chinese, used for almost all formal writing in China until the early 20th century. Each character usually corresponds to a single independent word, making the language terse and difficult for readers without literary training. From the 2nd century AD, Literary Chinese spread to [[Vietnam|Vietnam]], [[Korea|Korea]], [[Japan|Japan]], and the Ryukyu Islands, where it served as the common written language and as an international auxiliary language for administration and scholarship. Because its conservative tradition left many later spoken changes unrecorded, it is only partially intelligible when read aloud by those familiar only with modern forms.

Era of classical music, roughly 1750–1820, between the Baroque and Romantic periods. Its music is mainly homophonic, with a clear melody over subordinate chords, though [[Counterpoint|counterpoint]] remained important, and its style galant emphasized light elegance over Baroque grandeur. The [[Harpsichord|harpsichord]] declined as the main keyboard instrument, superseded by the [[Piano|piano]] (fortepiano), whose hammers allowed dynamic variation. The main instrumental forms were the [[Sonata|sonata]], string quartet, [[Symphony|symphony]], and solo [[Concerto|concerto]]; vocal forms included [[Opera|opera]] and songs. Joseph Haydn, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, and Ludwig van Beethoven all worked in [[Vienna|Vienna]], so the era is sometimes called Viennese Classicism.

Aesthetic attitude and art movement based on the culture of [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]] and Rome, emphasizing form, simplicity, proportion, clarity of structure, and restrained emotion. Classicism is a recurrent tendency in European traditions, with revivals in Carolingian and Ottonian art and in the [[Renaissance|Italian Renaissance]], when the fall of Byzantium and trade with Islamic cultures brought knowledge of antiquity. Renaissance architects returned to classical models, including the classical orders of [[Column|columns]] and the golden rectangle as a key proportion. In the 17th century, classicism took on more structural overtones of order, geometry, and rigorous discipline, and the court of Louis XIV was seen as its center. [[Neoclassicism|Neoclassicism]], an important movement of the [[Age of Enlightenment|Age of Enlightenment]], revived classical forms in the visual arts.

French [[Physiology|physiologist]] who originated the term *milieu intérieur* and the associated concept of homeostasis. I. Bernard Cohen of [[Harvard University|Harvard University]] called him "one of the greatest of all men of science." Walter Cannon coined the term homeostasis. His early work showed that the [[Pancreas|pancreas]] secretes a fluid containing an enzyme that splits neutral fats, and he found that introducing [[Ether|ether]] into the stomach or duodenum induced pancreatic secretions. In perhaps his most famous experiment, he discovered the glycogenic function of the [[Liver|liver]], which helped advance the study of [[Diabetes|diabetes]] mellitus. [[Napoleon III]] built him a laboratory in 1864, and in 1868 he was admitted to the Académie Française. When he died, he received a public funeral, which France had never allowed for a man of science.

French composer, sometimes seen as the first [[Impressionism|Impressionist]] composer, although he vigorously rejected the term. Born to a family of modest means, he was admitted to the Conservatoire de Paris at age ten and took many years to develop his mature style. He achieved international fame in 1902 with *Pelléas et Mélisande*, the only opera he completed. His orchestral works include *Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune* (1894), *Nocturnes* (1897–1899), and *La mer* (1903–1905). His music was to a considerable extent a reaction against Wagner and the German tradition, and he developed his own harmony and orchestral color. He was greatly influenced by Symbolist poetry. His piano works include 24 *Préludes* and 12 *Études*. Composers including [[Béla Bartók|Béla Bartók]], [[Igor Stravinsky|Igor Stravinsky]], and [[George Gershwin|George Gershwin]] were strongly influenced by his work.

French [[Anthropology|anthropologist]] and [[Ethnology|ethnologist]] who was a central figure in structuralism and structural anthropology. He argued that human minds share the same structures in all societies and that human characteristics are the same everywhere. His book *Tristes Tropiques* (1955) established his position in the structuralist school. Structuralism has been defined as "the search for the underlying patterns of thought in all forms of human activity." He held the chair of social anthropology at the Collège de France from 1959 to 1982 and was elected to the Académie française in 1973. His only ethnographic fieldwork, among Indigenous groups in Brazil, was conducted from 1935 to 1939 and informed his early analyses of [[Kinship|kinship]]. He won the 1986 International Nonino Prize.

French painter and founder of [[Impressionism|Impressionism]], seen as a key precursor to [[Modernism|modernism]]. He was the most consistent and prolific practitioner of Impressionism's aim of expressing perceptions of nature, especially in plein air landscape painting. The term derives from his painting *Impression, Sunrise*, exhibited in 1874 at the First Impressionist Exhibition. Raised in Le Havre, [[Normandy|Normandy]], he painted the same scene many times to capture changing light and the passing seasons, notably *Haystacks* (1890–1891) and *Rouen Cathedral* (1892–1894). From 1883 he lived in Giverny, where he created a water garden, and his [[Water Lilies (Monet series)|water lilies]] occupied him for the last 20 years of his life. His fame and popularity grew sharply in the second half of the 20th century.
